display_name: Plantagenet Omrah Pinot Noir, Great Southern
raw_content:
{
  "hook": "Great Southern's granite and gneissic sandy loams force Pinot Noir roots deep, yielding wines with mineral snap and red fruit purity. Plantagenet Omrah 2011 earned bronze medals at TEXSOM and unknown awards, signaling reliable quality from this cool corner of Western Australia. At 13 years old, it drinks with developed savory layers now.",
  "wine_summary": "Plantagenet crafts site-specific wines from Mount Barker in Great Southern, where maritime winds off the Southern Ocean temper summer heat for slow-ripening Pinot Noir. This 2011 Omrah reflects the producer's focus on single-vineyard expression amid 2,545 hectares of diverse sub-regions like Frankland River and Porongurup. Terroir here delivers brighter reds than warmer Aussie Pinots, with gravelly soils adding earthiness that sets it apart from fruit-forward Barossa styles.",
  "terroir_expression": "Lateritic gravelly sandy loams and karri loams in Great Southern's 0-1,083m elevation range promote drainage and mineral uptake, translating to graphite notes and firm structure in the glass. Cool maritime climate from the Southern Ocean—spanning 17,131 km² centered on Albany—locks in vibrant acidity and cherry skin flavors, while granite influences add wet stone persistence that lingers on the finish.",
  "vinification_summary": "Limited details exist on Omrah's exact process, but Plantagenet typically uses cool fermentation in small open fermenters to preserve fruit integrity, followed by French oak maturation for subtle spice integration. Wild yeast ferments, common in regional Pinots, build complex mid-palate texture without overpowering site character—oak here supports rather than dominates the terroir-driven profile.",
  "food_pairing": "Mushroom risotto absorbs the wine's earthiness from gneissic loams while acidity cuts creamy rice. Nashville hot chicken finds balance as Pinot's bright fruit tempers spice without clashing tannins. Coq au vin pairs via shared savory depth, with wine's mineral edge echoing braised chicken and mushrooms. Grilled salmon leverages cherry notes against fatty fish, acidity slicing through richness.",
  "comparable_wines": "Yering Station Little Yering Pinot Noir — matches cool-climate acidity and red fruit from Victorian soils. Bass Phillip Premium Pinot Noir — shares silky texture and earth from Gippsland, though more intense.",
  "style_profile": "Medium-bodied dry red with bright acidity and mineral earthiness",
  "cellar_recommendation": "Drink now through 2025 to catch secondary notes; store at 55°F away from light. Decant an hour before serving.",
  "value_assessment": "$30-45 AUD. Tasmanian Pinots like Tolpuddle or Yarra Valley's De Bortoli at the same price offer similar quality. Buy it for pure Great Southern expression that outpunches blended Aussies.",
  "market_position": "Somms on US coastal lists stock it for by-the-glass Aussie reds under $15 retail. Casual drinkers discovering cool-climate Pinot find it on specialty shelves next to Burgundy alternatives. Export markets favor it over hotter-climate rivals for food versatility.",
  "insider_take": "Most chase fruitier Pinots and miss this one's restraint—perfect if you value structure over jam. Skip for power styles; its finesse suits patient palates. Regional purists grab it before prices climb with Great Southern buzz.",
  "aging_potential_years": 15,
  "drinking_window_min_years": 8,
  "drinking_window_max_years": 15,
